propositions.text: Every taxpayer can arrange affairs to reduce tax payable, but tax planning must comply with the Income Tax Act and other statutes.
propositions.quote: Every taxpayer is entitled to order his or her affairs so that the tax payable is less than it otherwise would be. Taxpayers often engage in tax planning to achieve that result. Of course, if that tax planning is to achieve the desired result, it must be consistent with the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp .) (“ITA ”), and other statutes.

propositions.text: If tax planning violates statutory provisions, the intended tax minimization is not achieved, as in this appeal.
propositions.quote: If the planning runs afoul of such provisions, the sought after tax minimization is not achieved. That is the result in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states taxpayers can plan to reduce tax but must comply with the Income Tax Act; non-compliance means tax minimization fails, as here.

propositions.text: Two credit unions amalgamated into Envision Credit Union, seeking to avoid s. 87 ITA flow-through of tax attributes.
propositions.quote: In this case, two credit unions amalgamated into Envision Credit Union (“Envision”). In doing so, they sought to avoid the application of s. 87 of the ITA , which requires that certain tax attributes of amalgamating corporations “flow through” to the amalgamated corporation if specific criteria are met.

propositions.text: Avoiding flow-through would allow double claiming of capital cost allowance and lower tax rate on some income.
propositions.quote: By avoiding the flow-through of certain tax attributes, the credit union attempted to double claim capital cost allowance and would have an enhanced capacity for a lower tax rate on a portion of its income.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains two credit unions amalgamated into Envision, trying to avoid s. 87 ITA flow-through to double claim tax benefits.

propositions.text: Envision argues flow-through applies only if all property of predecessors becomes property of amalgamated corporation.
propositions.quote: Envision contends that the flow-through requirement applies only where “all of the property” of the amalgamating corporations becomes property of the amalgamated corporation.

propositions.text: Because some properties were sold at amalgamation, Envision says the flow-through precondition was not met.
propositions.quote: Envision argues that because certain properties were sold at the exact moment of the amalgamation, this precondition to flow-through was not met.

paragraphs.summary: Envision argues flow-through applies only if all property passes; selling some properties at amalgamation means flow-through precondition not met.

propositions.text: Envision could not avoid ITA flow-through by selling property at amalgamation because provincial statute caused ITA conditions to be fulfilled.
propositions.quote: I conclude that Envision was not able to avoid the application of the ITA rules by selling property at the time of amalgamation, because the provincial statute that permitted the amalgamation caused the ITA conditions to be automatically fulfilled.

propositions.text: The amalgamation met ITA flow-through requirements; appeal should be dismissed.
propositions.quote: The amalgamation therefore met the requirements for flow-through of tax attributes under the ITA . I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Envision could not avoid ITA flow-through by selling property; the amalgamation met flow-through requirements and appeal is dismissed.

propositions.text: On January 1, 2001, Delta and First Heritage credit unions amalgamated to form Envision for non-tax reasons but structured for tax benefit.
propositions.quote: On January 1, 2001, two British Columbia credit unions, Delta Credit Union (“Delta”) and First Heritage Savings Credit Union (“First Heritage”) (together the “predecessors”) amalgamated to form Envision. The merger was undertaken for non-tax reasons, but the transaction was structured to obtain the best possible tax outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states two BC credit unions amalgamated on Jan 1, 2001 to form Envision, structured for tax benefit though for non-tax reasons.

propositions.text: Amalgamation was under BC Credit Union Incorporation Act, which deems amalgamated credit union a continuation of predecessors and seized of all their property and liabilities.
propositions.quote: The amalgamation was carried out under the Credit Union Incorporation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 82 (“CUIA”). Under that Act, an amalgamated credit union is a continuation of the predecessor credit unions: ss. 20(1) and 23(a). The amalgamated credit union is “seized of” all the property and liabilities of its predecessors: s. 23(b).

propositions.text: Relevant CUIA and ITA provisions are in the attached Appendix.
propositions.quote: The relevant provisions of the CUIA and the ITA are in the attached Appendix.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the amalgamation was under BC law deeming the amalgamated credit union a continuation seized of all property and liabilities.

propositions.text: ITA distinguishes qualifying amalgamations under s. 87 with flow-through of tax attributes from non-qualifying amalgamations without specified tax consequences.
propositions.quote: Under the ITA , there are two types of amalgamations. “Qualifying amalgamations” are those that meet the requirements in s. 87 of the ITA . Once the s. 87 requirements are met, the ITA provides for the flow-through of various tax attributes while deeming a new taxation year and prohibiting the flow-through of other tax attributes. All other amalgamations, which are sometimes called “statutory amalgamations” or “non-qualifying amalgamations”, are outside the scope of s. 87 . The tax consequences of non-qualifying amalgamations are not specified in the ITA and therefore must be determined using the other provisions of the ITA , where relevant, other relevant statutes and the common law.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states ITA has qualifying amalgamations with s. 87 flow-through and non-qualifying amalgamations without specified tax consequences.

propositions.text: Qualifying amalgamation under s. 87 requires all property, liabilities, and shareholders of predecessors to become those of amalgamated corporation by virtue of merger.
propositions.quote: A qualifying amalgamation under s. 87 of the ITA has three basic requirements: (a) all of the property of the predecessor corporations immediately before the merger must become property of the amalgamated corporation (sometimes called “Amalco”) by virtue of the merger; (b) all of the liabilities of the predecessor corporations immediately before the merger must become liabilities of Amalco by virtue of the merger; and (c) all of the shareholders, who owned shares of the capital stock of any predecessor corporation immediately before the merger, must receive shares of the capital stock of Amalco because of the merger.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains s. 87 qualifying amalgamation requires all property, liabilities, and shareholders of predecessors to become those of amalgamated corporation.

propositions.text: Delta and First Heritage tried to avoid s. 87 by transferring beneficial interest in surplus properties to subsidiary 619 at amalgamation.
propositions.quote: In this case, Delta and First Heritage attempted to avoid the application of s. 87 and engage in a non-qualifying amalgamation by having the beneficial interest in certain real properties that were surplus to their business needs (the “surplus properties”) pass at the moment of amalgamation from the predecessors to a recently created subsidiary, 619547 B.C. Ltd. (“619”).

propositions.text: In exchange, 619 issued shares to predecessors, which flowed to Envision; Envision retained legal title as bare trustee but beneficial interest vested in 619.
propositions.quote: In exchange for those surplus properties, 619 issued shares to the predecessors, which then flowed through to Envision as a result of the amalgamation. Upon amalgamation, Envision retained the legal title to the surplus properties as a bare trustee, but the beneficial interest was vested in 619.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the predecessors transferred beneficial interest in surplus properties to subsidiary 619 at amalgamation; Envision held legal title as trustee.

propositions.text: Envision says its amalgamation was non-qualifying because not all property passed to it; beneficial ownership of surplus properties passed to 619.
propositions.quote: Envision took the position that its amalgamation was not a qualifying amalgamation because not all of the property of the predecessors had passed to Envision. Specifically, the beneficial ownership of the surplus properties passed to 619 and did not flow through to Envision.

propositions.text: Ownership of shares of 619 does not mean Envision owned 619's property; thus s. 87 flow-through provisions did not apply.
propositions.quote: While shares of 619 flowed to Envision, ownership of shares does not mean that Envision owned the property of 619: A.F., at para. 68, footnote 49. The provisions in s. 87 that provide for the flow-through of various tax attributes did not apply because all of the property of the predecessors did not flow through to Envision.

paragraphs.summary: Envision argues its amalgamation was non-qualifying because beneficial ownership of surplus properties passed to 619, so s. 87 flow-through did not apply.

propositions.text: Two tax attributes at issue are capital cost allowance (CCA) and preferred rate amount (PRA).
propositions.quote: Two particular tax attributes are at issue in this appeal: capital cost allowance (“CCA”) and the preferred rate amount (“PRA”).

propositions.text: PRA is used to calculate a tax credit; generally, a lower PRA is preferable as it increases income taxed at lower small business rate.
propositions.quote: It is sufficient to know that the PRA is an amount used to calculate a PRA tax credit and, as a general matter, it is preferable for taxpayers to have a lower PRA. The PRA tax credit has the effect of increasing the amount of income that is taxed at what is effectively the lower small business tax rate.

paragraphs.summary: The Court identifies CCA and PRA as key tax attributes; PRA tax credit benefits taxpayers with lower PRA by increasing income taxed at lower rate.

propositions.text: Envision says non-qualifying merger reset its PRA to zero, potentially increasing PRA tax credit.
propositions.quote: Envision says that as a result of the non-qualifying merger, its PRA was reset to zero, which would have the effect of potentially increasing its ability to claim the PRA tax credit.

propositions.text: Envision filed tax returns on this assumption but PRA reset did not benefit it in relevant years; PRA was reason for non-qualifying amalgamation.
propositions.quote: Although Envision filed its tax returns in accordance with this assumption, it is undisputed that the PRA reset did not benefit it in the tax years relevant to this appeal. Nevertheless, the PRA was the reason that the decision was made to pursue a non-qualifying amalgamation.

propositions.text: Envision also said CCA deductions were reset on amalgamation, but only for consistency with PRA treatment.
propositions.quote: Envision also took the position that the CCA deductions taken by its predecessors were reset upon amalgamation, although it says it adopted this position only for the purpose of “consistency” with its treatment of the PRA.

paragraphs.summary: Envision argues non-qualifying merger reset PRA and CCA deductions, though PRA reset did not benefit it; PRA motivated the merger.

propositions.text: CCA is a business deduction reflecting asset depreciation over years; assets grouped by class for CCA purposes.
propositions.quote: CCA is, of course, widely known in the legal and accounting communities. However, a brief explanation may be helpful for the discussion that follows. CCA is a business deduction that reflects the fact that while the costs of acquiring certain depreciable capital assets (like buildings, equipment, vehicles etc.) are incurred in one taxation year, the assets are in fact used over a period of years. Under the CCA scheme, assets are grouped in classes according to their type.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains CCA as a deduction reflecting depreciation of capital assets grouped by class over years.

propositions.text: Taxpayers deduct a percentage of undepreciated capital cost (UCC) of each asset class annually as CCA; UCC reduces by claimed CCA each year.
propositions.quote: Each year, a taxpayer is permitted to deduct a percentage (assigned by the ITA for each class) of the undepreciated capital cost (“UCC”) of each class. This amount that is deducted is what is called the CCA. The starting UCC for each class is determined based on the actual cost to the taxpayer of acquiring the assets in that class. Each year, the UCC is reduced based on the CCA that the taxpayer has claimed in that taxation year.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains CCA deduction is a percentage of UCC per class, with UCC reduced annually by claimed CCA.

propositions.text: Envision argued CCA claimed by predecessors did not flow through, so UCC could reset to original capital cost, allowing double claim.
propositions.quote: Consistent with its position that its PRA had been reset by the amalgamation, Envision argued that since any CCA claimed by the predecessor credit unions did not flow through to Envision, the opening balance of their UCC account could be reset to the actual original capital cost of the assets.

propositions.text: This reset meant UCC was about $51 million (original cost) instead of $20 million (predecessors' UCC at amalgamation).
propositions.quote: This “reset” meant that the UCC of Envision was set at approximately $51 million, the original cost of the assets to the predecessor credit unions, rather than approximately $20 million which was the total of the UCC balances of the two predecessor credit unions at the time of amalgamation.

paragraphs.summary: Envision argued CCA did not flow through, so UCC reset to original cost ($51M) instead of predecessors' UCC ($20M), allowing double claim.

propositions.text: Minister reassessed Envision for 2001-2004, asserting PRA and UCC should flow through from predecessors; Envision appealed.
propositions.quote: The Minister reassessed Envision for the years 2001, 2002, 2003 and 2004 on the basis that the PRA and the UCC should flow through from the predecessors to Envision. Envision appealed these reassessments.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the Minister reassessed Envision for 2001-2004, asserting PRA and UCC should flow through; Envision appealed.

propositions.text: Tax Court found s. 87 did not apply; predecessors could sell surplus properties at amalgamation due to continued legal personality.
propositions.quote: At the Tax Court, Webb J. (as he then was) concluded that s. 87 did not apply to this amalgamation. He found that the predecessors had the legal capacity to sell the surplus properties at the same time as the amalgamation, since the predecessors’ legal personalities were continued under the relevant legislation.

propositions.text: CUIA s. 20(2) allows parties to specify how amalgamation is carried out; predecessors agreed surplus properties would not become Envision's property at amalgamation.
propositions.quote: He considered the effect of the CUIA and concluded that since s. 20(2) provided that parties to an amalgamation can specify the manner of carrying the amalgamation into effect, it was open to the predecessors to agree that certain property would not become the property of Envision at the time of amalgamation.

propositions.text: CUIA s. 23(b) stating all property becomes amalgamated credit union's property is a default rule that can be contracted out.
propositions.quote: Essentially, he found that while s. 23(b) stated that all property of the predecessors becomes property of the amalgamated credit union, that was a default rule that the predecessors could (and in this case did) contract out of.

propositions.text: Therefore, s. 87 did not apply to this amalgamation.
propositions.quote: As a result, he held that s. 87 did not apply to this amalgamation.

paragraphs.summary: Tax Court found s. 87 did not apply; predecessors could sell surplus properties at amalgamation by contracting out of default rule.

propositions.text: Black and Decker requires continuation without subtraction for continuation model amalgamations like under CUIA.
propositions.quote: He found that this Court’s decision in R. v. Black and Decker Manufacturing Co., [1975] 1 S.C.R. 411, applied to this amalgamation with the effect that Envision, deemed by statute to be a continuation of its predecessors, could not argue that no CCA had been claimed by the predecessors. Black and Decker requires that amalgamated corporations created under the continuation model of amalgamation “continue without subtraction” of the predecessors (p. 422).

propositions.text: CUIA provides continuation model; Envision cannot adopt original capital cost without CCA deducted by predecessors.
propositions.quote: The CUIA provides for a continuation model of amalgamation and therefore it was not open to Envision to adopt only the original capital cost of the assets that it received from its predecessors and not also the CCA deducted on those assets.

paragraphs.summary: Tax Court applied Black and Decker: under continuation model, Envision must continue CCA deductions claimed by predecessors.

propositions.text: Provincial CUIA can impact tax calculation under federal ITA; similarity to s. 87 result is not a reason to differ.
propositions.quote: Webb J. also rejected the argument that the provincial CUIA could not impact how taxes were calculated under the federal ITA . He concluded that simply because applying Black and Decker to the facts of this case would generate the same result as s. 87 , this was not a reason to reach a different result.

propositions.text: UCC of Envision must be reduced based on CCA previously claimed by predecessors.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the UCC of Envision had to be reduced based on the CCA previously claimed by the predecessors.

paragraphs.summary: Tax Court held provincial CUIA affects federal tax calculation; Envision's UCC must be reduced by predecessors' CCA.

propositions.text: Minister's reassessment of Envision's 2001 return was statute barred; Minister did not appeal this.
propositions.quote: Finally, Webb J. held that the Minister’s attempt to reassess Envision’s 2001 return was statute barred. This conclusion was not appealed by the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: Tax Court found Minister's reassessment of 2001 return was statute barred; Minister did not appeal.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found s. 87 applied because predecessor property traced into Envision shares
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal found that s. 87 applied to this amalgamation because the property owned by the predecessors (the surplus properties) could be traced into property owned by Envision (the shares of 619).

propositions.text: Amalgamation changed form of ownership from surplus properties to shares of 619
propositions.quote: The amalgamation merely changed the form in which Envision held ownership of the surplus properties since the surplus properties were in effect converted into shares of 619.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found s. 87 applied as predecessor property became Envision shares, changing ownership form from surplus properties to shares of 619.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal agreed Tax Court that Black and Decker requires combined UCC balances adoption even if amalgamation not qualifying
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal also found that the Tax Court was correct that Black and Decker had the effect of requiring Envision to adopt the combined UCC balances of its two predecessors even if the amalgamation was not a qualifying one.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal agreed with the Tax Court that Black and Decker requires combined UCC balances adoption even if amalgamation is not qualifying.

propositions.text: Appeal raises three questions about qualifying amalgamation, UCC/PRA calculation, and GAAR applicability
propositions.quote: This appeal raises three questions: (1) Was the Envision amalgamation a qualifying amalgamation under s. 87 of the ITA ? (2) If the Envision amalgamation was not a qualifying amalgamation, how should Envision’s UCC and PRA be calculated? (3) If the Envision amalgamation was not a qualifying amalgamation and the ITA otherwise permits Envision to reset its UCC and PRA without reference to its predecessors, is the general anti-avoidance rule applicable to deny Envision the tax benefit flowing from that conclusion?

paragraphs.summary: The appeal raises three questions on qualifying amalgamation, UCC/PRA calculation, and GAAR applicability, posed by the Court.

propositions.text: Court need not answer questions 2 and 3 because it concludes amalgamation was qualifying
propositions.quote: In view of my conclusion described below, that this was a qualifying amalgamation, it is not necessary for the Court to answer questions 2 and 3.

propositions.text: Court leaves question of flow-through of tax attributes after non-qualifying amalgamation for another day
propositions.quote: I leave this question for another day.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes the amalgamation was qualifying, so it need not answer questions 2 and 3 and leaves some issues for another day.

propositions.text: Section 87 requirements are satisfied because Envision was seized of surplus properties at amalgamation
propositions.quote: In my view, the requirements of s. 87 are satisfied by this amalgamation because Envision was seized of the surplus properties at the moment of amalgamation.

propositions.text: Amalgamation was qualifying; parties could not exclude property from Envision by virtue of CUIA
propositions.quote: I conclude that it was not open to the parties, by virtue of the CUIA, to have some property that belonged to the predecessors not become property of Envision by virtue of the amalgamation.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds s. 87 requirements met as Envision was seized of surplus properties at amalgamation and parties could not exclude property under CUIA.

propositions.text: Section 23 of CUIA had not been interpreted by this Court before
propositions.quote: Section 23 of the CUIA has not previously been interpreted by this Court.

propositions.text: Court only has benefit of lower courts' reasons on s. 23 interpretation
propositions.quote: this Court has only the benefit of the reasons of the courts below.

propositions.text: Court is not bound by Tax Court decisions on statutory interpretation
propositions.quote: this Court is not bound by the decisions of the Tax Court on questions of statutory interpretation.

propositions.text: Court reaches opposite conclusion to Webb J. on meaning and effect of s. 23(b) CUIA
propositions.quote: I reach the opposite conclusion as to the meaning and effect of s. 23(b) of the CUIA.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes s. 23 of CUIA was uninterpreted by it before, is not bound by Tax Court, and reaches opposite conclusion to Webb J. on s. 23(b).

propositions.text: Section 23(b) CUIA states amalgamated credit union holds all property, rights, debts of predecessors
propositions.quote: Section 23(b) of the CUIA states: 23 On and after the date of the amalgamation . . . . . . (b) the amalgamated credit union is seized of and holds and possesses all the property, rights and interests and is subject to all the debts, liabilities and obligations of each amalgamating credit union . . . .

propositions.text: This language means amalgamated credit union owns all predecessor property
propositions.quote: This language provides that the result of an amalgamation under the CUIA is that the amalgamated credit union is the owner of all the property of its predecessors.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains s. 23(b) CUIA means the amalgamated credit union owns all property, rights, and liabilities of predecessors.

propositions.text: CUIA has no deeming rule for time of amalgamation on the date
propositions.quote: The CUIA provides no deeming rule for determining at what time on the date of the amalgamation that amalgamation takes place,

propositions.text: B.C. Business Corporations Act provides amalgamation occurs at beginning of date if no time specified
propositions.quote: unlike the B.C. Business Corporations Act, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57, s. 279(b)(ii), which provides that if no time is specified for the amalgamation, it occurs at the beginning of the specified date.

propositions.text: Parties agree amalgamation moment was commencement of January 1, 2001
propositions.quote: the parties are in agreement that the moment of amalgamation was set in the amalgamation agreement as the commencement of January 1, 2001.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes CUIA lacks a deeming time rule for amalgamation date, unlike B.C. Business Corporations Act; parties agreed on January 1, 2001 start.

propositions.text: Envision argues credit unions can contract around s. 23(b) effect for particular properties
propositions.quote: Envision argues that credit unions can contract around the effect of s. 23(b) with respect to particular properties.

propositions.text: Envision relies on s. 20 CUIA allowing terms and conditions of amalgamation to argue property can pass to third party
propositions.quote: Envision relies on s. 20 of the CUIA which permits amalgamating credit unions to specify “the terms and conditions of the amalgamation” and “the manner of carrying the amalgamation into effect”.

propositions.text: Envision says s. 23(b) applies only to property not otherwise provided for in amalgamation agreement
propositions.quote: Envision takes the position that s. 23(b) is only operative on property that the amalgamation agreement has not otherwise provided for.

propositions.text: Because predecessors agreed surplus properties pass to 619, s. 23(b) cannot cause Envision to be seized of them
propositions.quote: because the predecessor credit unions had agreed that the surplus properties would pass to 619, s. 23(b) could not cause Envision to be seized of those surplus properties.

paragraphs.summary: Envision argues it can contract around s. 23(b) effect for certain properties under s. 20, so surplus properties pass to 619, not Envision.

propositions.text: Section 23(b) is mandatory and not subject to contracting out by credit unions
propositions.quote: In my view, s. 23(b) is not a provision out of which amalgamating credit unions are permitted to contract.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds s. 23(b) is mandatory and credit unions cannot contract out of it.

propositions.text: Credit unions must amalgamate per s. 20 CUIA but s. 23 prescribes effects that cannot be overridden
propositions.quote: Credit unions in B.C. are not permitted to amalgamate except in accordance with the requirements of s. 20 of the CUIA. Section 20(2)(a)(ii) permits predecessors to set the terms and conditions of amalgamation. However, s. 23 describes the effects of a s. 20 amalgamation.

propositions.text: Terms and conditions under s. 20 cannot contradict or override s. 23 effects
propositions.quote: While s. 20 empowers predecessor credit unions to set terms and conditions of amalgamation, those terms and conditions cannot contradict or override the automatic consequences of amalgamation specified in s. 23 of the CUIA.

propositions.text: Nothing in s. 20 authorizes credit unions to set effects of amalgamation on assets or liabilities
propositions.quote: Nothing in s. 20 expressly provides authority for amalgamating credit unions to set their own effects or consequences of amalgamation with respect to assets or liabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds s. 20 allows setting terms but not overriding s. 23 effects on assets or liabilities in amalgamation.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Cromwell J. that s. 20 describes conditions and s. 23 describes effects of amalgamation
propositions.quote: In this respect, I am in agreement with Cromwell J. Section 20 describes the conditions for an amalgamation. Section 23 describes the effects.

propositions.text: Court disagrees that distinction between effects and conditions raises doubts about contracting out of s. 23(b)
propositions.quote: However, I cannot see how this distinction between effects and conditions of amalgamation raises doubts for my colleague about the conclusion that parties cannot contract out of the effects of s. 23(b).

paragraphs.summary: The Court agrees s. 20 sets conditions and s. 23 sets effects, and rejects doubts about contracting out of s. 23(b).

propositions.text: Allowing contracting out of s. 23 would undermine legislature's statutory scheme
propositions.quote: To permit amalgamating credit unions to contract out of s. 23 of the CUIA would undermine the statutory scheme constructed by the legislature.

propositions.text: Nothing in s. 20 or s. 23 permits contracting out of express statutory consequences of amalgamation
propositions.quote: Nothing in s. 20 or s. 23 of the CUIA permits amalgamating credit unions to contract out of any of the express statutory consequences of an amalgamation,

propositions.text: No common law power allows credit unions to amalgamate contrary to CUIA terms
propositions.quote: there is no independent common law power that permits credit unions to amalgamate in a manner that would contradict the terms of the CUIA.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds contracting out of s. 23 would undermine the statutory scheme and is not permitted by statute or common law.

propositions.text: Cromwell J. relies on explicit references to amalgamation agreement in s. 23(a) and (c) but not in (b)
propositions.quote: Cromwell J. relies on the fact that the other paragraphs in s. 23 contain explicit references to the amalgamation agreement: ...

propositions.text: Court finds absence of reference to amalgamation agreement in s. 23(b) suggests consequences cannot be altered by agreement terms
propositions.quote: If anything, it suggests the opposite conclusion: that the consequences prescribed by s. 23(b) cannot be altered by the terms of the amalgamation agreement.

propositions.text: s. 23(c) binding members to agreement does not imply agreement can override s. 23(b)
propositions.quote: Nor does s. 23(c), which simply makes the amalgamation agreement binding on the members of the credit unions, suggest that the terms of the amalgamation agreement may be inconsistent with s. 23(b).

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Cromwell J.'s reliance on agreement references in s. 23(a) and (c) does not support overriding s. 23(b) consequences.

propositions.text: Legislature's policy forbids contracting out of s. 23 effects to protect creditors
propositions.quote: The policy reasons of the legislature for not permitting contracting out of the effects of s. 23 can easily be understood. Protection for creditors is a key issue in an amalgamation.

propositions.text: If contracting out allowed, liabilities could be excluded from amalgamation, which is untenable
propositions.quote: If Envision’s reading of the statute were correct, there would be no reason that predecessor credit unions could not also opt out of the effect of s. 23(b) in respect of liabilities, by specifying that liabilities or obligations should not pass to the amalgamated credit union. This would be an untenable result.

propositions.text: Amalgamations are not intended to split liabilities from assets
propositions.quote: Amalgamations are not intended to permit corporations to split liabilities from assets.

propositions.text: s. 23(b) protects creditors especially as CUIA lacks specific creditor protection provisions like B.C. Business Corporations Act
propositions.quote: The role of s. 23(b) as a protection for creditors is even more important because the CUIA does not contain specific provisions that protect the interests of creditors as does the B.C. Business Corporations Act.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds legislature forbids contracting out of s. 23 to protect creditors and prevent splitting liabilities from assets.

propositions.text: Regulatory approval required for credit union amalgamation under s. 20(3)(b) CUIA
propositions.quote: I agree with Cromwell J. that regulatory approval is required for credit unions to amalgamate and that credit unions operate in a highly regulated environment.

propositions.text: Regulator's obligation is to check if amalgamation agreement is contrary to interests of credit unions or members
propositions.quote: the statutory obligation of the regulator in approving an amalgamation agreement is to determine whether the amalgamation agreement is “contrary to the interests of one or more of the amalgamating credit unions or its or their members”: CUIA, s. 20(3)(b).

propositions.text: Regulatory approval process does not focus on creditor protection
propositions.quote: While the regulator may be interested in the protection of creditors, this is not the focus of the regulatory approval process.

propositions.text: Section 23(b) remains important for creditor protection
propositions.quote: Section 23(b), then, remains as an important element of creditor protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds regulatory approval focuses on credit unions' interests, not creditors, so s. 23(b) remains key for creditor protection.

propositions.text: By s. 23(b), Envision was seized of surplus properties at amalgamation moment
propositions.quote: By virtue of s. 23(b), therefore, Envision was seized of the surplus properties at the exact moment of amalgamation.

propositions.text: This fulfills s. 87(1)(a) ITA condition as all predecessor property became Envision's by merger
propositions.quote: This caused the condition in s. 87(1) (a) of the ITA to be fulfilled. All of the property of the predecessors was property of Envision by virtue of the merger.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds s. 23(b) caused Envision to be seized of surplus properties at amalgamation, fulfilling s. 87(1)(a) ITA condition.

propositions.text: Envision argues this interpretation renders s. 87 property and liabilities requirements redundant
propositions.quote: Envision argues that this interpretation would render the requirements with respect to property and liabilities in s. 87 of the ITA redundant because it would be impossible to fail to meet them, as effectively all corporate amalgamation statutes in Canada provide for continuity in respect of assets and liabilities.

propositions.text: Court finds current corporate law provisions fulfilling ITA conditions does not require different interpretation
propositions.quote: The fact that the two conditions in the ITA will always be fulfilled because of current corporate law provisions does not require a different interpretation to be given to those corporate law statutes.

propositions.text: ITA imposes tax consequences based on corporate law but does not alter corporate law interpretation
propositions.quote: The ITA exists to impose tax consequences based on corporate law; it does not exist to cause those corporate laws to be interpreted differently.

paragraphs.summary: Envision argues s. 87 requirements become redundant; Court rejects, saying ITA imposes tax consequences but does not alter corporate law interpretation.

propositions.text: Envision amalgamation was qualifying; s. 87(2)(d) and 137(4.3)(b) ITA apply for flow-through of CCA and PRA
propositions.quote: The Envision amalgamation was a qualifying amalgamation. Subsections 87(2)(d) and 137(4.3)(b), the provisions of the ITA that provide for the flow-through of CCA and PRA, apply and Envision’s tax attributes must be adjusted accordingly.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes the Envision amalgamation was qualifying and ITA provisions for flow-through of tax attributes apply.

propositions.text: Cromwell J. argues s. 23(b) analysis unnecessary but it was basis of appeal argument
propositions.quote: Cromwell J. argues that the s. 23(b) analysis is unnecessary. However, it was the basis on which this appeal was argued both in this Court and in the courts below.

propositions.text: Parties made submissions on CUIA sections meaning and effect
propositions.quote: The parties made submissions on the meaning and effect of these sections of the CUIA.

propositions.text: Declining to decide issue after full process would create uncertainty; better to decide now
propositions.quote: I cannot see any advantage to declining to decide an issue after a full appeal process and complete submissions of the parties. Indeed, to the extent that practical problems should guide judicial decision making, I think those factors suggest that this Court decide this matter now rather than leaving the matter unresolved and therefore uncertain.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds s. 23(b) analysis was basis of appeal, parties fully argued it, and deciding now avoids uncertainty.

propositions.text: Section 23(b) of the CUIA caused the conditions in s. 87 of the ITA to be fulfilled, resolving the tax issue.
propositions.quote: The above analysis is sufficient to resolve the tax issue in this case, because s. 23(b) of the CUIA caused the conditions in s. 87 of the ITA to be fulfilled.

propositions.text: Envision argues the amalgamation agreement circumvented s. 23(b) of the CUIA.
propositions.quote: Envision raises the issue of the effectiveness of the amalgamation agreement which Envision argues was the mechanism by which s. 23(b) was circumvented.

propositions.text: If surplus properties could not avoid becoming Envision's property, the amalgamation agreement might be invalid.
propositions.quote: Envision argues that if it was not possible for Envision to structure its affairs so that the surplus properties did not become property of Envision, the amalgamation agreement between the predecessor credit unions might be invalid

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 23(b) of the CUIA fulfills s. 87 ITA conditions; Envision argues the amalgamation agreement circumvented s. 23(b) and might be invalid.

propositions.text: Tax consequences cannot be tailored to avoid negative corporate law consequences.
propositions.quote: Tax consequences which flow from the application of tax law cannot be tailored to avoid negative corporate law consequences.

propositions.text: Envision argues the Court's interpretation should consider effects on private transactions.
propositions.quote: Envision is arguing that the Court’s interpretation of s. 23(b) of the CUIA and s. 87 of the ITA should turn on the effect it would have on these parties’ private transaction

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Envision's argument that tax law interpretation should consider private transaction effects, stating tax consequences cannot be tailored.

propositions.text: Practical problems of invalidating a long-operational amalgamation may be significant but do not arise here.
propositions.quote: I agree that the practical problems posed by potentially invalidating an amalgamation that has been operational for over 10 years could be significant. However, I am not convinced that such practical problems arise in this case.

propositions.text: Despite Envision holding surplus properties at amalgamation, sale and amalgamation agreements were effective.
propositions.quote: Despite the fact that Envision was seized of the surplus properties at the time of amalgamation, an outcome that the predecessors were trying to avoid, the sale agreements and the amalgamation agreement were still effective.

propositions.text: Effect of agreements matched predecessors' plan except for tax consequences due to s. 23(b) of the CUIA.
propositions.quote: the effect of those agreements was identical to the effect that the predecessors had planned for, with the sole exception of the tax consequences which could not have been achieved because of s. 23(b) of the CUIA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no practical problems here; sale and amalgamation agreements were effective except for tax consequences due to s. 23(b).

propositions.text: Understanding purchase and sale agreements is necessary to understand the amalgamation agreement's operation.
propositions.quote: a proper understanding of the effect of these agreements is necessary to understand how the amalgamation agreement operated in this case.

propositions.text: Envision has not directly raised the effectiveness of purchase and sale agreements.
propositions.quote: Envision has not directly raised the issue of the effectiveness of the agreements for purchase and sale

paragraphs.summary: The court notes understanding purchase and sale agreements is necessary to understand the amalgamation agreement; Envision has not raised their effectiveness.

propositions.text: Two agreements provided for sale of surplus properties with vendors as Delta and First Heritage at amalgamation moment.
propositions.quote: Two agreements were entered into to provide for the sale of the surplus properties. These agreements were structured so that the vendors were Delta and First Heritage.

propositions.text: Envision argues vendors were predecessors who sold surplus properties, so Envision did not sell them to subsidiary.
propositions.quote: Envision argues that since the vendors were the predecessors they were the parties that sold the surplus properties. Therefore Envision did not and could not have sold the properties to the subsidiary.

propositions.text: The court disagrees with Envision's argument about vendors and sale of surplus properties.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree.

paragraphs.summary: The court states two sale agreements named predecessors as vendors; Envision argues predecessors sold properties, but the court disagrees.

propositions.text: At amalgamation, predecessors lost separate legal personality; obligations must be fulfilled by Envision per s. 23(b) of CUIA.
propositions.quote: At the moment of amalgamation, the predecessors, Delta and First Heritage, no longer had separate legal personalities capable of fulfilling the terms of the sale agreements... This is the effect of s. 23(b) of the CUIA

propositions.text: Despite vendors named as predecessors, at amalgamation the vendor was Envision.
propositions.quote: despite the fact that the agreements listed Delta and First Heritage as the vendors, at the moment of amalgamation, the vendor was Envision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds predecessors lost separate legal personality at amalgamation; Envision became vendor despite agreements naming predecessors.

propositions.text: Continuation model amalgamation means constituent companies lose separate existence but continue to exist.
propositions.quote: under a continuation model of amalgamation, “upon amalgamation each constituent company loses its ‘separate’ existence but it by no means follows that it has thereby ceased to exist”

propositions.text: Contracts entered by predecessors bind and must be fulfilled by amalgamated entity unless restricted.
propositions.quote: contracts that were entered into in the names of the predecessor corporations are binding upon and must be fulfilled by the amalgamated entity, barring restrictions in those contracts to the contrary

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Black and Decker: amalgamation causes loss of separate existence but contracts bind the amalgamated entity.

propositions.text: Sale agreements bind successors; successors include corporations formed by amalgamation.
propositions.quote: the agreements specifically state that they are binding on Delta and First Heritage’s successors... A corporation’s successor is generally understood to include those corporations formed as a result of an amalgamation

propositions.text: Successor corporations include those formed by amalgamation (Black’s Law Dictionary).
propositions.quote: A corporation’s successor is generally understood to include those corporations formed as a result of an amalgamation: Black’s Law Dictionary (9th ed. 2009).

propositions.text: Agreements were properly carried out by Envision at amalgamation as predecessors had no separate existence.
propositions.quote: since at the moment of amalgamation, Delta and First Heritage had no separate existence and because the contracts for sale of the surplus properties were binding on Envision, those agreements were properly carried out by Envision at that time.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds sale agreements bind successors including Envision, which properly carried out agreements at amalgamation.

propositions.text: Parties characterized case as simultaneous transactions but did not distinguish between sale and amalgamation events.
propositions.quote: The parties have characterized this case as being one of simultaneous transactions... the parties did not acknowledge the different nature of these two events.

propositions.text: Distinction exists between a transaction regarding property (sale) and a larger transaction affecting property (amalgamation).
propositions.quote: The distinction is between a transaction with respect to the properties (the sale) and a larger transaction that had an effect on the properties (the amalgamation).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds parties called this simultaneous transactions but failed to distinguish sale from amalgamation events.

propositions.text: Being seized of property is not a conveyance; amalgamation is continuation, not transfer.
propositions.quote: Envision’s seizure of the property cannot be equated to a conveyance: Black and Decker, at p. 417... continuation model of amalgamation

propositions.text: No time existed when predecessors and Envision coexisted as separate entities to convey property.
propositions.quote: there was no point in time when Delta, First Heritage and Envision existed as separate legal entities such that Delta and First Heritage could convey their property to Envision.

propositions.text: A conveyance requires separate legal entities at transfer time; here only Envision existed at amalgamation.
propositions.quote: A conveyance requires that the seller and the buyer be separate legal entities at the time of the transfer of the property... At the moment of amalgamation, only Envision continued to exist as a separate legal entity.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains seizure differs from conveyance; only Envision existed at amalgamation, so no conveyance occurred.

propositions.text: No prior court interpreted 'is seized of' in CUIA context; similar language in Company Act interpreted as continuation.
propositions.quote: No court has previously interpreted the phrase “is seized of” in the context of the CUIA... interpretations of that section suggest that the language ought to be considered as analogous to the provisions that this Court interpreted in Black and Decker

propositions.text: Manco Home Systems Ltd. interpreted similar language as continuation, not transfer.
propositions.quote: Interpretations of that section suggest that the language ought to be considered as analogous to the provisions that this Court interpreted in Black and Decker: Manco Home Systems Ltd., Re

propositions.text: Black and Decker concluded continuation model amalgamations are not transfers or conveyances of assets.
propositions.quote: this Court in Black and Decker concluded that continuation model amalgamations are not transfers or conveyances of assets.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no prior interpretation of 'is seized of' in CUIA; similar language interpreted as continuation, not transfer.

propositions.text: At creation, Envision was seized of property and able to fulfill predecessors' obligations, including selling surplus properties.
propositions.quote: At the moment that Envision was created, it was seized of the property and was immediately able to transact in relation to that property... required to fulfill the obligations of the predecessors, such as the obligation to sell the surplus properties to 619.

propositions.text: Sale agreements for surplus properties were effective.
propositions.quote: It follows that the agreements for the sale of the surplus properties were effective.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Envision seized property at creation and fulfilled obligations; sale agreements were effective.

propositions.text: Part 6.1 of amalgamation agreement states amalgamated credit union holds all property and obligations of predecessors.
propositions.quote: Part 6.1 of the amalgamation agreement between the predecessors provides: ... the Amalgamated Credit Union shall... be seized of and shall hold and possess all of the property, rights and interests, and shall be subject to all debts, liabilities and obligations, of each of Delta and First Heritage

propositions.text: Part 6.1 repeats effect of s. 23 of CUIA except for underlined text.
propositions.quote: This provision, with the exception of the underlined text, simply repeats the effect of s. 23 of the CUIA.

propositions.text: Part 8 provides predecessors will transfer surplus assets to a subsidiary at Effective Time.
propositions.quote: Part 8 provides that at the Effective Time, the predecessors will transfer certain surplus assets to a subsidiary.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Part 6.1 and Part 8 of amalgamation agreement about property seizure and surplus asset transfer.

propositions.text: Nothing in Part 8 conflicts with s. 23(b) of CUIA; predecessors' commitments fulfilled by Envision after amalgamation.
propositions.quote: There is nothing in Part 8 that is inconsistent with the requirements of s. 23(b) of the CUIA... actions undertaken to fulfil those commitments were undertaken by the amalgamated credit union, Envision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Part 8 consistent with s. 23(b) of CUIA; commitments fulfilled by Envision after amalgamation.

propositions.text: Part 6's 'subject to Part 8' means predecessors committed to selling surplus properties at amalgamation.
propositions.quote: The statement in Part 6, that the seizure of the assets is “subject to Part 8”, must be interpreted in light of the meaning of Part 8. The effect of Part 8 is to commit the predecessors to selling the surplus properties at the moment of amalgamation.

propositions.text: Nothing in Part 8 prevented Envision from being seized of surplus properties; it committed predecessors and Envision to sale.
propositions.quote: Nothing in Part 8 prevented Envision from being seized of the surplus properties upon amalgamation. Rather, it merely committed the predecessors and therefore Envision to making the sale.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Part 6 and 8 mean predecessors committed to selling surplus properties; Envision seized properties and made sale.

propositions.text: Extrinsic evidence of intent to prevent Envision seizure violates s. 23(b) of CUIA; lawful contract interpretation preferred.
propositions.quote: such an arrangement would be in violation of s. 23(b) of the CUIA... a lawful interpretation ought to be preferred over an unlawful one

propositions.text: When contract can be construed two ways, lawful interpretation preferred (G. McMeel).
propositions.quote: When a contract may be construed in two ways, a lawful interpretation ought to be preferred over an unlawful one: G. McMeel

propositions.text: Contract words best interpreted as ensuring sale at amalgamation time; amalgamation agreement not invalid.
propositions.quote: the words of the contract... are best interpreted as merely ensuring that the surplus properties were sold at the time of the amalgamation... the amalgamation agreement is not invalid.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds intent to prevent Envision seizure violates s. 23(b); contract interpreted lawfully ensuring sale; agreement not invalid.

propositions.text: No need to consider Court of Appeal's tracing approach; if considered, it must be rejected.
propositions.quote: it is unnecessary to consider the Court of Appeal’s approach of tracing the surplus properties through the shares of 619... the tracing approach would have to be rejected.

propositions.text: Basic company law rule: shareholders do not own company assets (Wotherspoon v. Canadian Pacific Ltd.).
propositions.quote: It is a basic rule of company law that shareholders do not own the assets of the company: see, e.g., Wotherspoon v. Canadian Pacific Ltd.

propositions.text: ITA look-through rules are explicit and do not support general tracing of assets to shareholders.
propositions.quote: While the ITA provides for “look-through” rules... those provisions are explicit

paragraphs.summary: The court finds tracing approach unnecessary and rejects it; shareholders do not own company assets; ITA look-through rules are explicit.

propositions.text: Minister argues broad property definition and s. 87 language create look-through or tracing rule.
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that the broad definition of property and the language in s. 87 of “in such a manner that” is sufficient to create such a look-through or tracing rule.

propositions.text: Court rejects Minister's argument; legislative language not explicit enough to create tracing rule.
propositions.quote: In my view, that cannot succeed. That legislative language is not as explicit as those provisions of the ITA that permit shareholders to be deemed to be the owners of corporate property.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Minister's argument that s. 87 creates tracing rule; language not explicit enough.

propositions.text: Due to s. 23(b) of CUIA, predecessors could not structure amalgamation to avoid s. 87(1)(a) ITA condition.
propositions.quote: As a result of s. 23(b) of the CUIA, it was not possible for the predecessors to structure an amalgamation that did not meet the condition in s. 87(1) (a) of the ITA.

propositions.text: Envision amalgamation qualifies under ITA; UCC balance and PRA must be determined per s. 87 ITA.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the Envision amalgamation was a qualifying amalgamation under the ITA and Envision’s UCC balance and PRA must be determined in accordance with s. 87 of the ITA.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 23(b) made the amalgamation qualify under ITA s. 87; Envision's UCC and PRA must be determined accordingly.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed with costs.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal with costs.

propositions.text: Appeal should be dismissed with costs, based on sequencing of events not reflected in the transaction.
propositions.quote: I agree with my colleague Rothstein J. that this appeal should be dismissed with costs.

propositions.text: At amalgamation, predecessor corporations ceased independent legal existence; only Envision existed as separate legal entity.
propositions.quote: at the moment that Envision was created, the predecessor corporations ceased to have any independent legal existence.

propositions.text: No time when Delta and First Heritage existed separately to convey property to Envision; only Envision was separate legal entity at amalgamation.
propositions.quote: there was thus no point in time when Delta Credit Union, First Heritage Savings Credit Union and Envision Credit Union existed as separate legal entities such that Delta and First Heritage could convey their property to Envision

propositions.text: This reasoning fully answers the appeal; analysis can stop here.
propositions.quote: That is sufficient to fully answer the appellant’s appeal and I would stop the analysis there.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes appeal should be dismissed because predecessor corporations ceased to exist independently at amalgamation, so no conveyance occurred.

propositions.text: Colleague relies on s. 23 CUIA to hold s. 23(b) prohibits contracting out of amalgamating credit unions.
propositions.quote: My colleague also relies on s. 23 of the Credit Union Incorporation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 82 (“CUIA”), to resolve the appeal by holding that s. 23(b) is a provision out of which amalgamating credit unions are not permitted to contract

propositions.text: Court finds it unnecessary and undesirable to adopt this interpretation of s. 23 in this case.
propositions.quote: I find it both unnecessary and undesirable to adopt this interpretation of s. 23 in this case.

propositions.text: Reasoning in para 61 suffices to resolve appeal; no need to speculate on alternative scenarios.
propositions.quote: it is not necessary to speculate on what would have happened if that were not the case.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds reliance on s. 23(b) unnecessary and undesirable since earlier reasoning suffices to resolve appeal.

propositions.text: Colleague interprets s. 23(b) as prerequisite for lawful amalgamation, requiring compliance with ITA s. 87(1)(a) and (b).
propositions.quote: My colleague interprets s. 23(b) of the CUIA as establishing a prerequisite to a lawful amalgamation.

propositions.text: This interpretation is significant but unsupported by authority and not approved by Tax Court judge.
propositions.quote: there is apparently no authority to support it (certainly none is cited) and it did not attract the approval of the learned Tax Court judge in this case

propositions.text: Concerns about correctness given statute text and structure; interpretation may cause practical problems.
propositions.quote: there is reason to be concerned about the correctness of the proposed interpretation given the text and structure of the statute.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes colleague's interpretation of s. 23(b) as prerequisite for lawful amalgamation lacks authority and raises concerns.

propositions.text: No authority cited by colleague; Court usually aided by other courts' reasons but none here.
propositions.quote: Rothstein J. cites none on this point — other than to observe that the Court is generally assisted by reasons of other courts on points that it decides.

propositions.text: Tax Court judge did not accept interpretation; suggests reasonable tax lawyers may differ on this point.
propositions.quote: his conclusion suggests that the interpretative point before us is at least one on which reasonable and highly experienced tax lawyers may reasonably differ.

propositions.text: Court will address statute text and structure raising doubts about colleague's interpretation.
propositions.quote: I will address in somewhat more detail the aspects of the text and structure of the statute that raise doubts in my mind as to the correctness of my colleague’s interpretation.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes absence of authority and Tax Court judge's disagreement, raising doubts about colleague's interpretation.

propositions.text: Colleague reads s. 23 as legal requirements for amalgamation, but comparison with s. 20 makes this doubtful.
propositions.quote: Rothstein J. reads s. 23 as setting out legal requirements for an amalgamation out of which the parties cannot contract.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds colleague's reading of s. 23 as legal requirements doubtful when contrasted with s. 20.

propositions.text: Legislature uses clear language in s. 20 to set legal requirements for amalgamation.
propositions.quote: Section 20 provides that two or more credit unions may amalgamate, “but must not do so except in accordance with this section”: s. 20(1).

propositions.text: Section 20 details substantive and procedural requirements including regulatory approval.
propositions.quote: There follows in s. 20 a detailed list of substantive and procedural requirements, including the need for regulatory approval.

propositions.text: Clear language in s. 20 shows intent to set legal requirements for amalgamation.
propositions.quote: It would be hard to find clearer expression of the intent to set out legal requirements.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 20 clearly sets legal requirements for amalgamation including regulatory approval.

propositions.text: Section 23 describes effects of amalgamation, not legal requirements for lawful amalgamation.
propositions.quote: Section 23 uses language that describes the effects of amalgamation; it does not use language that establishes requirements for a lawful amalgamation.

propositions.text: Section 23 premised on certificate issued and adopts terms of amalgamation agreement.
propositions.quote: Section 23 is premised on a certificate of amalgamation having been issued and it adopts the terms of the amalgamation agreement

propositions.text: Language in s. 23(b) is odd if meant as prohibition on contents of amalgamation agreement.
propositions.quote: It would also seem to be an odd approach to drafting to put a prohibition relating to the contents of an amalgamation agreement in s. 23(b)

propositions.text: S. 23 likely describes effects recognizing central role of amalgamation agreement, not conditions for amalgamation.
propositions.quote: there is reason to think that s. 23 does not set out the conditions for amalgamation; that is the role of s. 20.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds s. 23 describes effects of amalgamation, not conditions, unlike s. 20 which sets conditions.

propositions.text: CUIA structure shows similar provisions for acquisitions and amalgamations with conditions and effects separated.
propositions.quote: The provisions in the CUIA which deal with acquisitions (ss. 16 to 18) and amalgamations (ss. 20 to 24) have a similar structure.

propositions.text: Section 16 sets acquisition conditions like s. 20 sets amalgamation conditions; s. 18 describes effects like s. 23 does for amalgamation.
propositions.quote: Section 16 sets out the conditions for acquisition of a credit union by asset transfer in the same way that s. 20 sets out the conditions for amalgamation.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds CUIA structure separates conditions (ss.16,20) and effects (ss.18,23) for acquisitions and amalgamations.

propositions.text: Colleague concerned s. 23 interpretation needed to protect creditors of predecessor credit unions.
propositions.quote: My colleague is concerned that the interpretation of s. 23 he proposes is essential in order to address concerns that, without such a provision, creditors of predecessor credit unions would not, or might not be protected on amalgamation.

propositions.text: Section 20 addresses creditor protection via regulatory approval requirement.
propositions.quote: Section 20 addresses this concern, however, through the requirement for regulatory approval of the proposed amalgamation.

propositions.text: Credit unions operate in highly regulated environment; creditor protection unlikely to depend heavily on s. 23(b).
propositions.quote: credit unions operate in a highly regulated environment and it seems to me to be rather unlikely that creditor protection depends so heavily on s. 23(b).

paragraphs.summary: Court finds creditor protection addressed by s. 20 regulatory approval, not heavily dependent on s. 23(b).

propositions.text: Good reason to question colleague's interpretation of s. 23(b).
propositions.quote: Taking these points into account, there seems to me to be good reason to question the interpretation advanced by my colleague.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes there is good reason to question colleague's interpretation of s. 23(b).

propositions.text: Colleague acknowledges practical problems if amalgamation invalidated after 10 years.
propositions.quote: As he properly acknowledges in para. 43, “the practical problems posed by potentially invalidating an amalgamation that has been operational for over 10 years could be significant”.

propositions.text: No such problems arise here, but interpretation could cause significant problems in other cases.
propositions.quote: Although no such problems in fact arise here, I would not adopt an interpretation that is recognized to have the potential to give rise to significant practical problems in other cases

propositions.text: Deciding this point unnecessarily risks creating problems rather than solving them.
propositions.quote: deciding this point when it is unnecessary to do so is much more likely to create problems than to solve them.

paragraphs.summary: Court concerned about practical problems from colleague's interpretation and prefers not to decide unnecessarily.

propositions.text: Colleague's interpretation has far-reaching effects, no authority, text and structure difficulties, and practical problems.
propositions.quote: Rothstein J. proposes an interpretation: (1) that has potentially far-reaching effects beyond the construction of the CUIA; (2) in support of which no authority is offered; (3) which encounters some difficulty having regard to the structure and text of the statute; and (4) which is acknowledged to have the potential to cause significant practical problems in other cases.

propositions.text: Court should not adopt this interpretation when unnecessary for proper disposition of appeal.
propositions.quote: it is my view that the Court should not take this step when doing so is completely unnecessary for the proper disposition of the appeal before us.

paragraphs.summary: Court declines to adopt colleague's interpretation due to lack of necessity and multiple concerns.
